_nota: English text for tripulacion.html. actualizar_bd.py uses it to replace the Spanish names, units and facts. Facts keep the same order as data/salud-espacial/astronaut_health.json (efectos), then the three extra facts.
hechos: Night-time HR same as on Earth (55.5±7 vs 55.7±8 bpm in flight). (ISS long duration)
HR during daily activity on Earth: morning 71.0±13, afternoon 71.5±9, night 72.8±10 bpm (pre-flight reference). (ISS long duration)
HR and catecholamines unchanged for months on the ISS. (ISS long duration)
HR, blood pressure and baroreflex unchanged from pre-flight to flight. (ISS long duration)
After the flight, HR and cardiac output rise slightly. (ISS long duration)
On short flights, HR, diastolic pressure, its variability and ventricular extrasystoles go down. (Space Shuttle)
Modest cardiovascular changes: the heart beats more slowly in microgravity. (Inspiration4)
5 days after return, autonomic regulation of HR is still altered; after a month it has almost fully recovered. (ISS long duration)
24 h systolic BP: 120±10 before, 106±9 in flight, 122±13 at landing. (ISS long duration)
Diastolic BP unchanged during and after the flight. (ISS long duration)
24 h ambulatory pressure drops 8-10 mmHg due to a 39% fall in systemic vascular resistance. (ISS long duration)
The night-time drop in blood pressure (8±3 mmHg) is maintained in space. (ISS long duration)
Systemic vascular resistance -39%. (ISS long duration)
Stroke volume +35±10%. (ISS long duration)
Cardiac output +41±9%. (ISS long duration)
Baroreflex response falls by ~1/3 after the flight, only when seated. (ISS long duration)
With in-flight exercise and IV fluids at landing, none had orthostatic hypotension during daily activities. (ISS long duration)
Hypotension and presyncope in 20-30% of astronauts on return. (Space Shuttle)
6 of 11 crew members with stagnant or reversed jugular flow around day 50; one with a thrombus. (ISS long duration)
Resting increase of ~1 °C that develops gradually over 2.5 months, up to ~38 °C; linked to IL-1ra. (ISS long duration)
During exercise, core temperature rises higher and faster than on Earth; it often exceeds 40 °C. (ISS long duration)
Average of 6.09 h/night on the ISS (5.96 on the Shuttle) even though 8.5 h are scheduled. (ISS)
~3 months before the flight they were already sleeping less than 6.5 h/night. (Training)
24% of nights with >=7 h on the ISS (12% on the Shuttle) vs 50% and 42% after the mission. (ISS)
75% of ISS crew members and 78% of Shuttle crew members used sleep medication at some point. (ISS)
Spine aBMD -0.9%/month. (ISS long duration)
Hip aBMD -1.4 to -1.5%/month. (ISS long duration)
Hip trabecular vBMD -2.2 to -2.7%/month. (ISS long duration)
Calcaneus -0.4%/month. (ISS long duration)
Average loss of 1-1.5%/month at load-bearing sites; large variation between sites and crew members. (ISS long duration)
Some astronauts lose >10% at the hip and spine after 6 months. (ISS long duration)
Calf volume -13±2% (soleus -15%, gastrocnemius -10%). (ISS long duration)
Peak power -32% after the flight. (ISS long duration)
On the recent ISS, 2-5% of initial body mass is lost (Zwart 2014). (ISS long duration)
Linear model over 619 missions: -2.4% per 100 days (Matsumoto 2011). (619 missions)
Crew members consume on average 80% of the recommended energy. (ISS long duration)
Actual average load 43 min/day versus 146.8 min assigned. (ISS long duration)
~10% of the fluid in the blood vessels is lost on arrival in space. (ISS long duration)
54% more red blood cell destruction (3 vs 2 million/s) throughout the mission. (ISS long duration)
One year later it is still 30% above the pre-flight level; red blood cells normal after 3-4 months. (ISS long duration)
5 of 13 astronauts with diagnosable anemia at landing. (ISS long duration)
Effective dose ~0.2 to ~0.5 mSv/day or more. (ISS)
Mean effective dose of 72 mSv per ~6-month mission. (ISS)
Career limit 600 mSv; 250 mSv per solar particle event. (-)
~66% of long-duration astronauts show early signs of SANS (spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome). (ISS long duration)
61% of ISS astronauts shed reactivated herpesviruses; few have symptoms. (ISS)
Each 1 mmHg of CO2 doubles the probability of headache; <=4 mmHg halves the weekly risk. (ISS)
One day after landing, the functional circuit takes 48% longer; deficits for up to a week. (ISS long duration)
Low body mass, carotid distension and greater intima-media thickness, eye changes, gene expression and cognitive changes; most return to pre-flight levels. (ISS long duration)
Space motion sickness: affects 60 to 80 % of astronauts in the first 2 or 3 days and usually resolves within 72 hours.
Back pain from adapting to space: incidence of 52 % (382 of 728 astronauts), mild in 86 % of cases; the fetal position (knees to chest) brought relief in 91 %.
Medical care on the ISS: there is a crew medical officer, flight surgeons on Earth with private medical conferences, a defibrillator on board, and evacuation is possible within hours.
